title: Reconstruction & Rebuild in Peoria, AZ | Gold Water Fire | Phoenix, AZ Metro
description: Reconstruction and rebuild for Peoria, AZ homes after water or fire damage. Gold Water Fire, AZ ROC #264344, KB-2. Call (480) 999-3339.
intro: The drying equipment is gone and the house is quiet again, and what is left is a room with no drywall on the lower two feet, a kitchen with the cabinets pulled off the wall, and a stack of paperwork you have read four times. You have been the one making every call, tracking every number, deciding what gets thrown out. Nobody warned you that the hardest part would come after the emergency ended, when the adrenaline is gone and the house still is not a house.

sections.heading: Putting the house back is a separate job from drying it out
sections.body: Mitigation stops the damage and removes what cannot be saved. Reconstruction is everything after: hanging and finishing drywall, resetting baseboard and casing, rebuilding cabinet boxes and countertops, replacing flooring, repainting, reinstalling fixtures, and getting the electrical and plumbing points back where they belong. These are different trades with different scheduling and different inspection requirements, which is why so many homeowners get stranded in between. At Gold Water Fire, reconstruction work is led by Brandon Gurr, our Construction Manager, with Johnny as Reconstruction Team Lead. We carry AZ ROC license #264344, KB-2. If your loss started with a burst line or a roof leak, the water damage restoration side of the work has to be genuinely finished, verified dry, before the rebuild begins. Closing up a wall over damp framing is how a Peoria homeowner ends up doing this twice.

sections.heading: What we see in Peoria houses
sections.body: Peoria is really two building eras stacked on top of each other, and they fail in different ways. The older core near Grand Avenue and Old Town has block and stick-built homes on slab with cast iron or galvanized supply, single-pane openings, and additions done over decades. When those homes flood, the rebuild almost always turns up something not to current code inside the wall. North of the Loop 101, out through Vistancia, Sonoran Mountain Ranch, Fletcher Heights and the Lake Pleasant Parkway corridor, the stock is newer production housing: two-story, engineered wood truss and I-joist floor systems, wide-open great rooms, tile roofs, and a second-floor laundry or upstairs bathroom sitting directly over the main living space. A supply line failure up there does not stay upstairs. Water runs the joist bays, drops through can lights, and takes out ceiling drywall, insulation, and flooring on two levels at once. Those big open floor plans also mean matching flooring becomes a real design decision, not a patch, because the tile or LVP runs uninterrupted from the entry to the back slider.

cards.heading: Monsoon and the roof
cards.body: July through September, outflow winds ahead of a storm lift tile and expose underlayment, and then the rain arrives. Peoria sits where those storms come off the desert to the west and northwest with little to slow them. The interior damage usually shows up as a ceiling stain days later, after the underlayment has been wicking the whole time.

cards.heading: Water heaters in the garage
cards.body: Common in newer Peoria subdivisions. A tank failure runs across the garage slab and under the shared wall into the hall or bedroom carpet. The rebuild is drywall, base, insulation, sometimes a door jamb, plus flooring that has to tie back into what is already there.

cards.heading: Second-story laundry
cards.body: Standard in a lot of the north Peoria two-story plans. A failed washer hose or pan drain sends water through the floor system into the ceiling below. Expect ceiling and wall drywall on the lower level, insulation, and paint carried to a natural break so the repair does not read as a patch.

cards.heading: Hard water and older supply
cards.body: Valley water is hard, and in the older Peoria homes with aging galvanized or early CPVC, small joint leaks run behind a vanity or under a kitchen sink for a long time before anyone notices. That is a cabinet, subfloor, and often a section of wall, not just a stain.

sections.heading: You should not have to be the general contractor of your own house
sections.body: Most homeowners we meet in Peoria have already done more than their share. They shut off the water at the meter, moved furniture at midnight, pulled wet carpet themselves, sent the photos, wrote the list. The reason it makes sense to hand off the rebuild is not that you cannot do it. It is that reconstruction after a loss is a scheduling problem more than a building problem: drywall has to be dry before it is hung, paint has to follow finish carpentry, flooring has to follow paint in some cases and precede it in others, and every one of those trades has to show up in the right order or the whole thing slides by weeks. That sequencing is what our team does. Brooke handles water and mitigation scheduling, Kristine keeps the office and paperwork side moving, and Brandon and Johnny run the build. Gold Water Fire was started by Jim Bennett and Jake Taylor, and you can read more about the people doing the work on our about page.

sections.heading: Fire losses and the paperwork side
sections.body: A fire damage rebuild in Peoria adds layers a water loss does not have. Smoke travels the return air path and settles in places the flames never reached, so scope often extends past the visibly burned rooms into HVAC, attic insulation, and finishes throughout. Structural members that were heat-affected have to be evaluated and, where needed, replaced or sistered before anything closes up. Peoria permits and inspects through the city, and rebuild work of that scope typically means permits and inspections before drywall goes back. On the insurance side, the useful thing to understand is that adjusters work from a line-item scope, so anything not written down does not get paid for. Photographs of what was behind the wall, the make and model of what was removed, and the finish grade of what was there before all matter. Keep receipts. Keep the old cabinet door if you can. Our reconstruction and rebuild service page covers the broader process across the metro.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to rebuild after water damage in Peoria?
faqs.a: It depends on scope. Replacing drywall, paint, and flooring in kind often does not require one. Work that touches structure, electrical circuits, gas, or plumbing rough-in generally does, and the City of Peoria handles permitting and inspection for properties inside city limits. If your rebuild includes any of that, the permit and inspection steps get built into the schedule rather than discovered late.

faqs.q: Can you match flooring that is no longer made?
faqs.a: Sometimes, and when not, the honest answer is that a partial replacement will show. In open Peoria floor plans where tile or plank runs continuously from the entry through the great room, the usual approaches are sourcing remaining stock, transitioning at a natural break like a doorway or hallway, or replacing the full continuous run. We walk through those options with you before anything is ordered so the outcome is not a surprise.

There is no honest single answer, because it depends on the size of the affected area, whether structure or systems are involved, permit and inspection timing, and material lead times on things like cabinets and specialty flooring. What we can do is give you a sequence and tell you what each step is waiting on, so you always know where the job stands rather than wondering.

faqs.q: Do you serve all of Peoria?
faqs.a: Yes. We cover the full Phoenix metro area, with a boundary the owner describes as NW Peoria, SE Avondale, SW San Tan Valley, NW Apache Junction, and outlying areas further than that. That includes Old Town Peoria, Fletcher Heights, Sonoran Mountain Ranch, Vistancia, and the Lake Pleasant Parkway corridor, along with neighboring Glendale, Surprise, and El Mirage.
